roadmap.goal: Story #6053 — an over-time chart shows the trend the instance's stored work items already support, instead of the handful of days the forward-only recorder happened to catch (4 recorded days against ~365 reconstructible ones on the dev database). A series read detects the days it is missing inside the window it was asked for and asks for them; a filler of this feature's own computes each missing day with the recorder's own code and a shifted window, writes it only if absent, and never touches the request thread. Four phases mirroring the four story slices: 01 cycle time at thirty days, team scope, where every mechanism is established (the decorator seam, the filler and its registration shape, the maintenance-gate coupling in both directions, the data floor, the last-observation ceiling, the absence gate on BOTH write paths, the ninety-day cap with an enforced wall-clock budget, and the unique-index collision backstop on a real SQLite file); 02 the other two look-backs, work item age at the NoHorizon sentinel, and portfolio scope; 03 the process-behaviour families at both scopes with the today-anchored baseline threaded to an explicit as-of day; 04 the honest empty states, the widget copy, and the metrics documentation. Done when: all 41 pending acceptance cases across Slice05-Slice08 are un-ignored and green, the one already-green pin stays green, the backend builds with zero warnings and the suite is green with the live-connector categories excluded, `pnpm test` and `pnpm build` are clean, SonarQube Cloud reports no new issue of any severity, and Stryker kill rate is >= 80% on the changed backend surface run last on frozen code.

user_decisions: D1 — reconstruct, never synthesize. A missing day D is the recorder's own service call with the window shifted to (D − horizon, D), stamped RecordedAt = D. DemoPercentilesBackfillHandler invents values and stays demo-only and untouched.
D2 — the trigger is the series read detecting a gap in the window it was asked for. The endpoints stay read-only in their RESPONSE and acquire the right to ask.
D3 — the read never blocks on reconstruction. It enqueues and returns the series as it stands; the chart fills on a later load.
D4 / DDD-6 — the walk stops at the data floor, and at a cap of 90 days PER PASS (not 90 days of reach) plus a wall-clock budget. A year-wide picker fills across successive loads.
D5 — leading and interior gaps are filled on one code path with no gap taxonomy; the ceiling is the owner's UpdateTime, because a broken-connection owner's items are frozen at the break.

D6 — no flag, no dashed segment, no tooltip difference between a reconstructed point and a recorded one. Confirmed for the mechanism by SPIKE-01 (4/4); fidelity across a CONFIGURATION change remains unprobed and is carried as OQ-1.

D7 / DDD-13 — never write an all-zero percentile row, on BOTH the reconstruction path and the shipped forward recorder. The second half is a behaviour change to shipped code, accepted in the open; rows already written stay, with no repair migration.

DDD-1 — the unit of reconstruction is (owner, window), never (owner, family, day). One ask per owner per read covering every family for that scope, which is what makes 'switching tabs does not re-trigger' structural.

DDD-2 / DDD-3 — the trigger lives in a decorator over each series query port. IOverTimeGapReconciler has one void method and holds no repository, so 'a GET wrote to the database on the request thread' is not representable from the read side.

DDD-4 — the carrier is a filler of this feature's own, not IUpdateQueueService. The queue is one channel with one reader (ADR-195's three lanes shipped and were reverted with story-5877), a new UpdateType is a user-visible cancellable Task-Manager row, and an admitted key holds database maintenance off.

DDD-9 / DDD-10 — one day-writer per table with two NAMED operations, RecordToday (overwrites) and FillDayIfAbsent (writes only if absent), never one operation with a mode flag. The family descriptors move into the writer so the family set is one list rather than an agreement between two.

DDD-12 — every today-anchor on the process-behaviour path becomes an explicit as-of day defaulting to Clock.Today. Additive, so the forward recorder and all six point-in-time widgets stay byte-identical. A pinned-baseline owner's correct series is flat limits, NOT an empty one.

DDD-17 / DEVOPS-1 / G-5 / G-6 — the maintenance gate and the filler see each other in BOTH directions, and it lands in phase 01 because phase 01 is the first thing that writes a row. One direction alone leaves the check-then-act race IUpdateStatusStore.CancelIfStillWaiting's own doc warns about.

DEVOPS-2 / G-7 / G-8 — the wall-clock budget is the longest a RestoreBackup may be held waiting, which is a question about operator patience and does not move with instance size. It must be ENFORCED: a pass that exceeds it abandons.

DEVOPS-3 — the pass-failed log template is pinned, not shaped: Error, "Over-time reconstruction pass failed for {OwnerType} {OwnerId} ({MetricFamily})", props OwnerType, OwnerId, MetricFamily, Exception, with MetricFamily carrying the recorders' own two values.
DEVOPS-4 — the filler is deliberately invisible on the operator surface. No Task-Manager row, no progress bar, no cancel button; the log line is the only operator signal.

Orphaned snapshot rows from deleted owners (the dev DB carries 7 percentile rows and 4 PBC rows for an owner id that exists in neither Teams nor Portfolios). A real defect found while measuring this story; it belongs in its own bug.

Any new table, route, DTO, request or response field, EF migration, RBAC gate, external integration or technology. The design establishes none, which is why there is no coexistence matrix and no client version gate.

Adding a hasHistory-style boolean or any other discriminated-envelope field to the series response. ADR-108 has rejected that twice; it must be re-decided there, not slipped in through an empty-state fix.
Admitting the filler to IUpdateStatusStore, giving it an UpdateKey or an UpdateType, or adding a Task-Manager row. Every one of these reopens all four of DDD-4's reasons.

phases.name: The trend a team's data already supports
phases.description: Story slice 01, Slice05 tests: cycle time at thirty days, team scope. The decisive phase — it establishes every mechanism the other three reuse. The reconstruction seam (decorator over the query port, void-returning reconciler, a filler of this feature's own), the registration shape that makes the filler observable from an acceptance test at all, the maintenance-gate coupling in both directions, the data floor and the last-observation ceiling, the absence gate on BOTH write paths, the ninety-day cap with an enforced wall-clock budget, and the unique-index collision backstop proven against a real SQLite file. criteria: Idempotency is three layers and they are all present, because each catches what the others cannot: the in-flight key set collapses two asks in one process, fill-if-absent refuses to overwrite a day that already has a value, and the unique natural key on the table is the backstop when two processes get past both. Two replicas can both run a pass — that is wasted CPU, never a duplicate row and never a wrong value.

The unique-constraint violation is absorbed PER DAY, not per pass. A collision on one day must not abandon the other eighty-nine; that is the difference between a race that costs nothing and a race that costs a window.

These scenarios run against the real SQLite FILE the harness already uses, and nowhere else. Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory does not enforce unique indexes, so the same test written in the unit suite would pass against an implementation with NO backstop whatsoever. If a version of this check appears under the unit suite, delete it — it is worse than no test.

AReconstructionPassHeldInFlight() holds a pass genuinely open and releases it on Dispose. Both this step and 01-04 depend on it, so it is implemented here; a version that merely returns a no-op disposable makes 01-04's gate scenarios pass vacuously.

No SQLITE_BUSY surfaces while a fill and a refresh write concurrently. The 10 000 ms busy_timeout is a ceiling, not a guarantee, and this is the step where that distinction is checked rather than assumed.
A_refresh_landing_mid_fill asserts BOTH that every day in the window is present and that every day is held exactly once. Neither half alone would catch a writer that wins by overwriting.
steps.implementation_notes: Do not reach for a distributed lock or IUpdateExecutionLock. The unique index already makes duplicate work harmless, and buying a cross-replica lock against a harmless duplicate costs an UpdateKey and therefore an UpdateType that must never be admitted — an invariant with nothing enforcing it. If this step finds SQLITE_BUSY under realistic contention, STOP and report rather than widening the timeout: that is the finding the gate exists to surface, and it can still change the design at this point in the phase. criteria: The gate's new dependency exposes exactly ONE read-only member: is a pass in flight right now. It carries no UpdateKey, no UpdateType, no Task-Manager row, and it changes IUpdateStatusStore not at all. It is a single-member capability, not a second status store — anything wider reopens, one by one, the four reasons the update queue was rejected.

The blocked reason names the filler in its own case, so an operator is told WHAT is holding the operation rather than only that something is. DatabaseMaintenanceGate produces that message at two sites — the BlockedReason property and the TryAcquire early return — and both must agree; a message that differs by entry point is how an operator learns to distrust it.

The filler checks BEFORE EACH DAY, not once at the start of the pass. Abandoning mid-pass is free here and nowhere else in the system: each day is an independent write, already-written days stay, and the walk resumes because a read will happen again. That property is what makes per-day checking affordable, and it is specific to this component.

The filler NEVER acquires the gate. It defers to a maintenance operation; it does not become one. If it acquired the gate it would block backup and restore outright, which is a strictly worse failure than the one being fixed.

Both scenarios are un-ignored together. Shipping one direction is the check-then-act race the item exists to close, and a half-wired implementation would make the gate scenario green while the window stays open.
The existing DatabaseMaintenanceGate tests stay green. A gate that refuses maintenance when nothing is running is a worse bug than one that permits it, because nobody can clear it.
ThenStartingADatabaseRestoreIsAllowedAgain() must pass after the held pass disposes. A predicate that latches true is indistinguishable from a broken gate to the operator standing in front of it.
